core: The working definition of a political system: the structures through which a society organizes power and decision-making
The classic types: democracy, authoritarianism, monarchy, and theocracy, each described factually in one line
The distribution question: who rules — one person, few, or many (the classic one/few/many framing)
Regime versus government: rules of the game versus current players, with an original example
The mixed reality: real systems blend types, with an original example
The honest framing: every political system is a bet on how to organize power
supporting: The tradeoffs perspective on government action and public policy
Elitism versus pluralism as rival answers to who actually governs
Oligarchy and totalitarianism as members of the authoritarian family
The U.S. Constitution (Article I) as an example of a written framework that persists across changes of officeholders
outOfScope: Political sociology — power, authority, and the state as social institutions (sociology subject)
Elections, parties, and institutions of specific systems (sibling topics)

claims.claim: A political system is the set of structures through which a society organizes power and decision-making; OpenStax American Government 3e defines government as the means by which a society organizes itself and allocates authority to accomplish collective goals, and Britannica defines a political system as the formal legal institutions that constitute a government or state, including actual as well as prescribed political behavior.
In a democracy, people govern themselves, directly or through elected representatives.
In a monarchy, one ruler, usually a hereditary ruler, holds political power; in some monarchies the ruler's power is limited by law and the monarch rules alongside an elected legislature.

In a theocracy, government is by divine guidance or by officials regarded as divinely guided; government leaders are often members of the clergy, and the state's legal system is based on religious law.

Authoritarianism is a family of systems in which power is concentrated in a single leader or a small group not accountable to the voters; oligarchy (rule by a handful of elite members) and totalitarianism (government control over all aspects of citizens' lives) are members of this family.
The classic one/few/many classification groups political systems by the number of rulers: monarchies are rule by one, oligarchies rule by a few, and democracies rule by many.

The regime (the framework of rules and institutions through which power is exercised) is distinct from the government (the people holding office at a given time); Britannica's taxonomy of political change separates a change of leaders from a structural revision or radical revolution of the system.

The U.S. Constitution is a written framework that persists while officeholders change: Article I vests all legislative powers in a Congress of the United States and provides that House members are chosen every second year by the people.

Real political systems blend types: constitutional monarchies combine a monarch whose power is limited by law with an elected legislature, and representative systems include direct-democracy elements such as referendums and town meetings.

Government action and public policy are shaped by an ongoing series of tradeoffs and compromises rather than by any single formula, so every political system can be understood as a bet on how to organize power that wins some things and gives up others.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether authoritarianism is one system type or a family of types. OpenStax American Government 3e presents monarchy, oligarchy, totalitarianism, and democracy as separate forms of government, while the classic one/few/many scheme folds them together by ruler count, and Britannica's classification also separates autocratic from nonautocratic rule.
positions: OpenStax 3e 1.1 lists oligarchy and totalitarianism as distinct nondemocratic forms alongside monarchy and democracy.
Britannica's classification schemes group systems by number of rulers (one/few/many) and separately by autocratic versus nonautocratic rule.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats authoritarianism as a family of systems (including oligarchy and totalitarianism), names each type factually, and defers the full treatment of authoritarianism to its sibling topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a political system should be defined narrowly (formal legal institutions) or broadly (including actual behavior and interactions).
positions: Britannica offers both: the formal legal institutions that constitute a government or state, and, more broadly, actual as well as prescribed forms of political behavior.
OpenStax emphasizes how a society organizes itself and allocates authority to accomplish collective goals.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson adopts the broad working definition — structures through which a society organizes power and decision-making — and attributes it to both sources.
